brief.title: Relocatable solar for a hospital on the move
brief.persona: Dr. Chukwuemeka is an orthopaedic surgeon here. Grid power arrives for about six hours a day and drops without warning. When it fails mid-procedure, the theatre waits while staff start the diesel generator — and fuel now costs more than the hospital can afford.
brief.persona_note: Persona is illustrative, drawn from the brief.
brief.framing: An asset-mobility and financing problem as much as a power problem: solar and storage can run the theatres; the hard part is a system the hospital can move in five years, and a funder willing to pay for it.
constraints: Surgical theatres must have uninterrupted power, including during switchover
Nothing permanently attached to the current buildings; the system must move to the new site in about five years
Federal asset rules: the hospital cannot dispose of solar assets tied to its current buildings
Little or no upfront capital from the hospital
Keep diesel as backup until the new system proves itself
Maintainable by the hospital's engineering team or a local provider

deliverables.text: Critical-load list and phased design that powers surgical theatres first
Relocatable system design (ground-mounted or containerised) with a move plan for the new building
Ownership and financing model (lease or energy-as-a-service) that fits federal asset rules
Cost model comparing diesel, grid and solar over five and ten years
Funding pitch naming specific funders and the case for each

starter_questions: Which loads must never lose power, and which can wait for the grid?
How do you build a system that can move to a new building in five years?
Who should own the system so the hospital avoids asset-disposal problems?
Can diesel savings alone repay the system, and over how long?
Which funders have backed similar projects, and what do they require?
